title: Comprehensive Guide to sampleSizeCalc
text: Use case: Comparing means two independent groups (e.g., treatment vs. control) Example: clinical trial comparing mean blood pressure reduction two treatments Interpretation: - Need 37 subjects per group - Total sample size: 74 subjects - effect size (Cohen’s d): 0.67 Formula: \[n = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}) \cdot \sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2}\right)^2\] Reference: Chow et al. (2017). Sample Size Calculations Clinical Research (3rd ed.). CRC Press.
code: result <- sample_size_calculator(   design = "twoMeans",   mean1 = 10, # Control group mean (mmHg reduction)   mean2 = 12, # Treatment group mean (mmHg reduction)   sd = 3, # Common standard deviation   alpha = 0.05, # Significance level   power = 0.8 # Target power (80%) )  print(result) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Two independent samples, mean comparison" #> • Sample size per group: 37 #> • Total sample size: 74 #> Formula (plain text): #> `n = 2 * ((Z_alpha/2 + Z_beta) * sd / (mean1 - mean2))^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n = 2\left(\frac{Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}}{\delta}\right)^2 = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}) \cdot \sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2}\right)^2$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State hypotheses: H0: mu1 = mu2 vs H1: mu1 != mu2 (two-sided alpha = #> 0.05, power = 0.80). #> • Step 2: Calculate mean difference delta = |mu1 - mu2| = |10 - 12| = 2; common #> SD sigma = 3. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96 (for two-sided alpha = #> 0.05), Z_beta = 0.8416 (for power = 0.80). #> • Step 4: Compute initial sample size via normal approximation: n0 = 2 * #> ((Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta) * sigma / delta)^2 = 2 * ((1.96 + 0.8416) * 3 / 2)^2 = #> 35.32. #> • Step 5: Refine via exact two-sample Student's t-test power iteration #> (accounting for degrees of freedom df = 2n - 2). #> • Step 6: Round up to integer: n = 37 per group, total sample size N = 74. #> Reference: #> Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). *Sample size calculations in clinical research* (3rd ed.). CRC Press. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

title: Comprehensive Guide to sampleSizeCalc
text: Use case: Comparing means paired matched observations (e.g., pre-post measurements, matched pairs) Example: Measuring cognitive function intervention subjects Interpretation: - Need 29 pairs (.e., 58 measurements 29 subjects) - Standardized effect size: 0.62 Reference: Rosner (2015). Fundamentals Biostatistics (8th ed.). Cengage Learning.
code: result <- sample_size_calculator(   design = "pairedMeans",   meanDiff = 2.5, # Mean difference (post-pre)   sdDiff = 4.0, # SD of differences   alpha = 0.05,   power = 0.9 )  print(result) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Paired means" #> • Pairs needed: 29 #> • Total individuals: 58 #> Formula (plain text): #> `n = ((Z_a/2 + Z_b) * sd_diff / mean_diff)^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n = \left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}) \cdot \sigma_d}{\mu_d}\right)^2$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State paired difference hypotheses: H0: mu_d = 0 vs H1: mu_d != 0 #> (alpha = 0.05, power = 0.90). #> • Step 2: Expected paired difference mu_d = 2.50, SD of differences sigma_d = #> 4. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 1.2816. #> • Step 4: Normal approximation: n0 = ((Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta) * sigma_d / #> mu_d)^2 = ((1.96 + 1.2816) * 4 / 2.50)^2 = 26.90. #> • Step 5: Exact paired Student's t-test degrees of freedom iteration. #> • Step 6: Round up to integer: n = 29 pairs (total individuals = 58). #> Reference: #> Rosner, B. (2015). *Fundamentals of biostatistics* (8th ed.). Cengage Learning. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

title: Comprehensive Guide to sampleSizeCalc
text: Use case: Comparing proportions two independent groups Example: Comparing response rates two treatments Interpretation: - Need 163 patients per group - Absolute risk reduction: 0.15 - Relative risk increase: 50% Reference: Fleiss et al. (2003). Statistical Methods Rates Proportions (3rd ed.). Wiley.
code: result <- sample_size_calculator(   design = "twoProportions",   p1 = 0.30, # Control response rate   p2 = 0.45, # Treatment response rate   alpha = 0.05,   power = 0.8 )  print(result) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Two independent proportions" #> • Sample size per group: 163 #> • Total sample size: 326 #> Formula (plain text): #> `n = (Z_a/2 * sqrt(2*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) + Z_b * sqrt(p1*(1-p1)+p2*(1-p2)))^2 / #> (p1-p2)^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{2\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1) + p_2(1-p_2)}\right]^2}{(p_1 - p_2)^2}$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State hypotheses: H0: p1 = p2 vs H1: p1 != p2 (two-sided alpha = #> 0.05, power = 0.80). #> • Step 2: Compute pooled proportion: p_bar = (p1 + p2) / 2 = (0.30 + 0.45) / 2 #> = 0.375. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416. #> • Step 4: Compute Fleiss formula numerator components: #> Z_(alpha/2)*sqrt(2*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) = 1.3419; Z_beta*sqrt(p1(1-p1)+p2(1-p2)) = #> 0.5693. #> • Step 5: Calculate unrounded sample size per group: n = (1.3419 + 0.5693)^2 / #> (0.30 - 0.45)^2 = 162.33. #> • Step 6: Round up to integer: n = 163 per group, total sample size N = 326. #> Reference: #> Primary (formula as implemented, without continuity correction): Fleiss, J. L., Tytun, A., & Ury, H. K. (1980). A simple approximation for calculating sample sizes for comparing independent proportions. Biometrics, 36(2), 343-346. #>  #> With continuity correction: Casagrande, J. T., Pike, M. C., & Smith, P. G. (1978). An improved approximate formula for calculating sample sizes for comparing two binomial distributions. Biometrics, 34(3), 483-494. #>  #> Book: Fleiss, J. L., Levin, B., & Paik, M. C. (2003). Statistical methods for rates and proportions (3rd ed.). Wiley. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

title: Comprehensive Guide to sampleSizeCalc
text: Use case: Time--event analysis log-rank test Example: Oncology trial comparing overall survival two treatments Important Notes: - calculates number events needed, total sample size - Total sample size = events / event rate - example, event rate 50%, total sample size needed: 494 subjects Formula: \[E = \frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta})^2}{p_E(1-p_E)[\ln(HR)]^2}\] Reference: Schoenfeld (1983). Sample-size formula proportional-hazards regression model. Biometrics, 39(2), 499-503.
code: result <- sample_size_calculator(   design = "survival",   hr = 0.70, # Hazard ratio (treatment vs. control)   pE = 0.50, # Proportion in experimental group (1:1 randomization)   alpha = 0.05,   power = 0.8 )  print(result) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Survival (log-rank)" #> • Events needed: 247 #> Formula (plain text): #> `E = (Z_a/2 + Z_b)^2 / (pE*(1-pE)*log(HR)^2)` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$E = \frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta})^2}{p_E(1-p_E)[\ln(HR)]^2}$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State survival parameters: Hazard Ratio HR = 0.70, experimental arm #> allocation pE = 0.50 (alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80). #> • Step 2: Compute log hazard ratio: ln(HR) = ln(0.70) = -0.3567. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416. #> • Step 4: Apply Schoenfeld formula: E = (Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta)^2 / [pE * (1 - #> pE) * (ln HR)^2] = (1.96 + 0.8416)^2 / [0.50 * 0.50 * (-0.3567)^2] = 246.79. #> • Step 5: Round up to integer: Target events needed E = 247. #> Reference: #> Primary: Schoenfeld, D. A. (1983). Sample-size formula for the proportional-hazards regression model. Biometrics, 39(2), 499-503. #>  #> Extensions: #> - Hsieh, F. Y., & Lavori, P. W. (2000). Sample-size calculations for the Cox proportional hazards regression model with nonbinary covariates. Controlled Clinical Trials, 21(6), 552-560. #> - Rubinstein, L. V., Gail, M. H., & Santner, T. J. (1981). Planning the duration of a comparative clinical trial with loss to follow-up and a period of continued observation. Journal of Chronic Diseases, 34(9-10), 469-479. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

title: Comprehensive Guide to sampleSizeCalc
text: Use case: Demonstrating new treatment worse standard margin Example: Non-inferiority trial new antidepressant Key Points: - Uses one-sided α (typically 0.025) - Margin Δ defines clinically acceptable difference - New treatment must within Δ standard Reference: Chow et al. (2017). Sample Size Calculations Clinical Research (3rd ed.). CRC Press.
code: result <- sample_size_calculator(   design = "nonInferiorityMeans",   mean1 = 8.0, # New treatment mean   mean2 = 8.5, # Standard treatment mean   sd = 2.0, # Common SD   margin = 1.0, # Non-inferiority margin (Δ)   alpha = 0.025, # One-sided test   power = 0.9 )  print(result) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Non-inferiority (means)" #> • Sample size per group: 337 #> • Total sample size: 674 #> Formula (plain text): #> `n = 2*(Z_a+Z_b)^2*sd^2/(mean1-mean2+margin)^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha} + Z_{\beta})\sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2 + \Delta}\right)^2$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State non-inferiority hypotheses: H0: mu1 - mu2 <= -margin vs H1: mu1 #> - mu2 > -margin (margin Delta = 1, one-sided alpha = 0.025, power = 0.90). #> • Step 2: Effective difference: delta_E = mu1 - mu2 + margin = 8 - 8.50 + 1 = #> 0.50; SD sigma = 2. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: one-sided Z_alpha = 1.96, Z_beta = 1.2816. #> • Step 4: Compute sample size: n = 2 * (Z_alpha + Z_beta)^2 * sigma^2 / #> delta_E^2 = 2 * (1.96 + 1.2816)^2 * 2^2 / (0.50)^2 = 336.24. #> • Step 5: Round up to integer: n = 337 per group, total sample size N = 674. #> Reference: #> Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). *Sample size calculations in clinical research* (3rd ed.). CRC Press. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

title: Comprehensive Guide to sampleSizeCalc
text: Use case: Demonstrating new treatment better standard Example: Superiority trial new pain medication Key Points: - Uses one-sided α - Effect must exceed margin meaningful - Smaller margin requires larger sample size
code: result <- sample_size_calculator(   design = "superiorityMeans",   mean1 = 12.0, # New treatment mean (better)   mean2 = 10.0, # Standard treatment mean   sd = 2.5, # Common SD   margin = 0.5, # Minimal clinically important difference   alpha = 0.025, # One-sided test   power = 0.85 )  print(result) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Superiority (means)" #> • Sample size per group: 50 #> • Total sample size: 100 #> Formula (plain text): #> `n = 2*(Z_a+Z_b)^2*sd^2/(mean1-mean2-margin)^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha} + Z_{\beta})\sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2 - \Delta}\right)^2$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State superiority hypotheses: H0: mu1 - mu2 <= margin vs H1: mu1 - #> mu2 > margin (margin Delta = 0.50, one-sided alpha = 0.025, power = 0.85). #> • Step 2: Effective difference: delta_E = mu1 - mu2 - margin = 12 - 10 - 0.50 = #> 1.50; SD sigma = 2.50. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: one-sided Z_alpha = 1.96, Z_beta = 1.0364. #> • Step 4: Compute sample size: n = 2 * (Z_alpha + Z_beta)^2 * sigma^2 / #> delta_E^2 = 2 * (1.96 + 1.0364)^2 * 2.50^2 / (1.50)^2 = 49.88. #> • Step 5: Round up to integer: n = 50 per group, total sample size N = 100. #> Reference: #> Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). *Sample size calculations in clinical research* (3rd ed.). CRC Press. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

title: Comprehensive Guide to sampleSizeCalc
text: Use case: Demonstrating two treatments equivalent Example: Bioequivalence study Key Points: - Uses TOST (Two One-Sided Tests) procedure - Requires Zβ/2 (larger sample size) - Margin must larger observed difference
code: result <- sample_size_calculator(   design = "equivalenceMeans",   mean1 = 100, # Test mean   mean2 = 102, # Reference mean   sd = 5, # Common SD   margin = 5, # Equivalence margin (±5 units)   alpha = 0.05,   power = 0.8 )  print(result) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Equivalence (means)" #> • Sample size per group: 48 #> • Total sample size: 96 #> Formula (plain text): #> `n = 2*(Z_a+Z_b/2)^2*sd^2/(margin-|mean1-mean2|)^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha} + Z_{\beta/2})\sigma}{\Delta - |\mu_1 - \mu_2|}\right)^2$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State equivalence hypotheses (TOST): H0: |mu1 - mu2| >= margin vs H1: #> |mu1 - mu2| < margin (margin Delta = 5, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80). #> • Step 2: Margin clearance: Delta - |mu1 - mu2| = 5 - |100 - 102| = 3; SD sigma #> = 5. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: one-sided Z_alpha = 1.6449, Z_(beta/2) = #> 1.2816. #> • Step 4: Compute sample size: n = 2 * (Z_alpha + Z_(beta/2))^2 * sigma^2 / #> (Delta - |mu1 - mu2|)^2 = 2 * (1.6449 + 1.2816)^2 * 5^2 / (3)^2 = 47.58. #> • Step 5: Round up to integer: n = 48 per group, total sample size N = 96. #> Reference: #> Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). *Sample size calculations in clinical research* (3rd ed.). CRC Press. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

title: Comprehensive Guide to sampleSizeCalc
text: Use case: Estimating sensitivity specificity given precision Example: Validating new diagnostic test disease X Interpretation: - Target state cases needed: 196 - Total subjects screen: 980 - 20% prevalence, need screen 980 get 196 cases Formula: \[n_{cases} = \frac{Z_{1-\alpha/2}^2 \cdot p(1-p)}{d^2}\] Reference: Hajian-Tilaki (2014). Sample size determination diagnostic test studies. Journal Biomedical Informatics, 48, 193-204.
code: result <- sample_size_calculator(   design = "diagnosticAccuracySingle",   prob = 0.85, # Expected sensitivity   d = 0.05, # Desired precision (±5%)   prevalence = 0.20, # Disease prevalence   alpha = 0.05 )  print(result) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Diagnostic accuracy (single)" #> • Cases needed: 196 #> • Total subjects to screen: 980 #> Formula (plain text): #> `N_cases = (Z_1-a/2)^2 * P*(1-P)/d^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n_{{{cases}}} = \frac{Z_{1-\alpha/2}^2 \cdot p(1-p)}{d^2}$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: Specify diagnostic accuracy prob (Se or Sp) = 0.85, margin of error d #> = 0.05, prevalence = 0.20 (alpha = 0.05). #> • Step 2: Determine critical value: Z_(1-alpha/2) = 1.96 (confidence level = #> 95%). #> • Step 3: Calculate target cases required: n_cases = Z_sum^2 * prob * (1 - #> prob) / d^2 = (1.96)^2 * 0.85 * 0.15 / (0.05)^2 = 195.91. #> • Step 4: Adjust for disease prevalence: total subjects to screen = n_cases / #> prevalence = 195.91 / 0.20 = 979.57. #> • Step 5: Round up to integer: Target cases needed = 196, Total subjects to #> screen = 980. #> Reference: #> Primary: Hanley, J. A., & McNeil, B. J. (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143(1), 29-36. #>  #> Review: Hajian-Tilaki, K. (2014). Sample size estimation in diagnostic test studies of biomedical informatics. Journal of Biomedical Informatics, 48, 193-204. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

title: Comprehensive Guide to sampleSizeCalc
text: Use case: Estimating AUC confidence interval given width Example: Validating new biomarker’s discriminative ability Key Points: - Calculates cases disease - AUC variance depends AUC value prevalence - Hanley-McNeil method standard approach Reference: Hanley & McNeil (1982). meaning use AUC. Radiology, 143(1), 29-36.
code: result <- sample_size_calculator(   design = "auc_single",   auc = 0.80, # Expected AUC   d = 0.05, # Half-width of CI (±0.10 total)   prevalence = 0.30,   alpha = 0.05 )  print(result) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Single-group AUC CI precision" #> • Cases needed: 373 #> • Total subjects to screen: 1243 #> Formula (plain text): #> `N_cases = (Z_1-a/2 / d)^2 * Var(AUC)` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n_{cases} = \left(\frac{Z_{1-\alpha/2}}{d}\right)^2 \cdot Var(AUC)$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: Specify anticipated AUC = 0.80, desired precision d = 0.05, #> prevalence = 0.30 (alpha = 0.05). #> • Step 2: Hanley-McNeil variance components: Q1 = AUC/(2-AUC) = 0.6667, Q2 = #> 2*AUC^2/(1+AUC) = 0.7111. #> • Step 3: Compute variance factor: V(AUC) = 0.2425. #> • Step 4: Calculate cases needed: n_cases = (Z_(1-alpha/2) / d)^2 * V(AUC) = #> (1.96 / 0.05)^2 * 0.2425 = 372.68. #> • Step 5: Adjust for prevalence: screening total = n_cases / prevalence = #> 372.68 / 0.30 = 1242.27. #> • Step 6: Round up to integer: Target cases needed = 373, Total subjects to #> screen = 1243. #> Reference: #> Primary: Hanley, J. A., & McNeil, B. J. (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143(1), 29-36. #>  #> Review: Hajian-Tilaki, K. (2014). Sample size estimation in diagnostic test studies of biomedical informatics. Journal of Biomedical Informatics, 48, 193-204. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

title: Comprehensive Guide to sampleSizeCalc
text: Use case: Comparing AUCs two diagnostic tests applied subjects Example: Comparing two imaging modalities Key Points: - Requires correlation coefficient (r) - Higher correlation → smaller sample size - Uses Hanley-McNeil method paired design
code: result <- sample_size_calculator(   design = "aucComparison",   auc1 = 0.85, # Test 1 AUC   auc2 = 0.80, # Test 2 AUC   r = 0.6, # Correlation between AUCs   prevalence = 0.25,   alpha = 0.05,   power = 0.8 )  print(result) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "AUC comparison (two tests)" #> • Cases needed: 545 #> • Total subjects to screen: 2179 #> Formula (plain text): #> `n_cases = 2 * (Z_alpha/2 + Z_beta)^2 * V(AUC) * (1 - r) / (AUC1 - AUC2)^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n_{cases} = \frac{2(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta})^2 \cdot V(AUC) \cdot (1-r)}{(AUC_1 - AUC_2)^2}$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: Specify AUC1 = 0.85, AUC2 = 0.80, correlation r = 0.60, prevalence = #> 0.25 (alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80). #> • Step 2: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416. #> • Step 3: Evaluate pooled Hanley-McNeil variance V(AUC_avg). #> • Step 4: Calculate target cases: n_cases = 2 * (Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta)^2 * #> V(AUC) * (1 - r) / (AUC1 - AUC2)^2. #> • Step 5: Round up to integer: Target cases needed = 545, Total subjects to #> screen = 2179. #> Reference: #> Hajian-Tilaki, K. (2014). Sample size estimation in diagnostic test studies of biomedical informatics. *Journal of Biomedical Informatics*, 48, 193-204. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbi.2014.02.013 #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

title: Comprehensive Guide to sampleSizeCalc
text: Use case: Sample size case-control studies odds ratio Example: Case-control study investigating smoking lung cancer Interpretation: - Cases needed: 80 - Controls needed: 80 - Total subjects: 160 Reference: Schlesselman (1982). Case-Control Studies: Design, Conduct, Analysis. Oxford University Press.
code: result <- sample_size_calculator(   design = "caseControl",   p0 = 0.30, # Exposure rate in controls   OR = 2.5, # Target odds ratio   m = 1, # Controls per case (1:1 matching)   alpha = 0.05,   power = 0.8 )  print(result) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Case-control" #> • Cases needed: 80 #> • Controls needed: 80 #> • Total subjects: 160 #> Formula (plain text): #> `n_cases = [Z_alpha/2 * sqrt((1+1/m)*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) + Z_beta * sqrt(p1*(1-p1) #> + p0*(1-p0)/m)]^2 / (p1 - p0)^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n_{cases} = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{(1+1/m)\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1) + p_0(1-p_0)/m}\right]^2}{(p_1-p_0)^2}$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: Compute case exposure rate from Odds Ratio: p1 = (OR * p0) / (1 - p0 #> + OR * p0) = (2.50 * 0.30) / (1 - 0.30 + 2.50 * 0.30) = 0.5172. #> • Step 2: Weighted average exposure (matching ratio m = 1): p_bar = (p1 + m*p0) #> / (1 + m) = 0.4086. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416. #> • Step 4: Schlesselman formula for cases: n_cases = #> [Z_(alpha/2)*sqrt((1+1/m)*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) + Z_beta*sqrt(p1*(1-p1) + #> p0*(1-p0)/m)]^2 / (p1 - p0)^2 = 79.19. #> • Step 5: Calculate controls needed: n_controls = m * n_cases = 1 * 79.19 = #> 79.19. #> • Step 6: Round up to integer: Cases needed = 80, Controls needed = 80, Total #> subjects = 160. #> Reference: #> Primary: Schlesselman, J. J. (1982). Case-control studies: Design, conduct, analysis. Oxford University Press. #>  #> IARC classic: Breslow, N. E., & Day, N. E. (1980). Statistical methods in cancer research: Volume I - The analysis of case-control studies. IARC Scientific Publications No. 32. #>  #> For individually matched designs (not the formula implemented here): Dupont, W. D. (1988). Power calculations for matched case-control studies. Biometrics, 44(4), 1157-1168; see the caseControlMatched design. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

title: Comprehensive Guide to sampleSizeCalc
text: Default print() output already includes four report components. summary() expands report input parameters, design axes available, recorded adjustments. summary includes: Study design description parameters used Sample size results Formula plain text LaTeX source Calculation process Literature references Parameter roles recorded adjustments available
code: result <- sample_size_calculator(   "survival",   hr = 0.70,   alpha = 0.05,   power = 0.8 )  summary(result) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Summary #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Study Design #> • Type: "Survival (log-rank)" #>  #> ── Parameters #> • hazard_ratio: 0.7 #> • allocation_ratio: 0.5 #> • alpha: 0.05 #> • power: 0.8 #>  #> ── Sample Size Results #> • Events needed: 247 #>  #> ── Formula #> Plain text: #> `E = (Z_a/2 + Z_b)^2 / (pE*(1-pE)*log(HR)^2)` #> LaTeX: #> $$E = \frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta})^2}{p_E(1-p_E)[\ln(HR)]^2}$$ #>  #> ── Calculation Process #> • Step 1: State survival parameters: Hazard Ratio HR = 0.70, experimental arm #> allocation pE = 0.50 (alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80). #> • Step 2: Compute log hazard ratio: ln(HR) = ln(0.70) = -0.3567. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416. #> • Step 4: Apply Schoenfeld formula: E = (Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta)^2 / [pE * (1 - #> pE) * (ln HR)^2] = (1.96 + 0.8416)^2 / [0.50 * 0.50 * (-0.3567)^2] = 246.79. #> • Step 5: Round up to integer: Target events needed E = 247. #>  #> ── Reference #> Primary: Schoenfeld, D. A. (1983). Sample-size formula for the proportional-hazards regression model. Biometrics, 39(2), 499-503. #>  #> Extensions: #> - Hsieh, F. Y., & Lavori, P. W. (2000). Sample-size calculations for the Cox proportional hazards regression model with nonbinary covariates. Controlled Clinical Trials, 21(6), 552-560. #> - Rubinstein, L. V., Gail, M. H., & Santner, T. J. (1981). Planning the duration of a comparative clinical trial with loss to follow-up and a period of continued observation. Journal of Chronic Diseases, 34(9-10), 469-479. #> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

text: Sample Size Calculator Clinical Research comprehensive R package sample size determination across 39 design combinations: experimental trials (superiority / non-inferiority / equivalence), observational studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional), diagnostic accuracy studies (estimation, testing, comparison, AUC), complex designs (cluster RCT, Simon two-stage, bioequivalence, ordered outcomes, prediction models, interrupted time series). Every result displays formula plain text LaTeX, calculation process, literature references default R console output. Parameter roles methodological hints included available.

title: Sample Size Calculator for Clinical Research
text: Scenario 1 — Antihypertensive RCT (continuous endpoint). cardiology trial compares new drug placebo systolic blood pressure reduction. Based phase-2 study, placebo arm expected drop 10 mmHg new drug 12 mmHg, pooled SD 3 mmHg (two-sided \(\alpha = 0.05\), 80% power). many patients per arm? Scenario 2 — H. pylori eradication RCT (binary endpoint). Standard triple therapy eradicates 70% infections; new bismuth quadruple regimen expected reach 85%. Scenario 3 — Generic vs originator antihypertensive (bioequivalence). \(2\times2\) crossover study healthy volunteers, intra-subject CV = 25%, expected geometric mean ratio \(\theta_0 = 1.0\), standard 80–125% acceptance range (Philips 1990 exact TOST). Scenario 4 — Colorectal cancer screening kit (diagnostic accuracy). Expected sensitivity 85%, required CI half-width \(\pm 5\%\), clinic prevalence 20%: many confirmed cases many screens? Scenario 5 — Diabetes prevalence survey (single proportion). Anticipated prevalence 30%, absolute precision \(\pm 5\%\), 95% CI (Bhardwaj 2024 worked example). Unambiguous designs allow omitting task/outcome: Illegal combinations error list legal ones. English guide Chinese guide cover design choices, parameters, formulas, worked clinical examples. regression tests check sample sizes published examples.
code:
library(sampleSizeCalc)  # design x task x outcome calculate("rct", "test", "mean",   mean1 = 10, mean2 = 12, sd = 3 ) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Two independent samples, mean comparison" #> • Sample size per group: 37 #> • Total sample size: 74 #> Formula (plain text): #> `n = 2 * ((Z_alpha/2 + Z_beta) * sd / (mean1 - mean2))^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n = 2\left( rac{Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{ eta}}{\delta}ight)^2 = 2\left( rac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{ eta}) \cdot \sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2}ight)^2$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State hypotheses: H0: mu1 = mu2 vs H1: mu1 != mu2 (two-sided alpha = #> 0.05, power = 0.80). #> • Step 2: Calculate mean difference delta = |mu1 - mu2| = |10 - 12| = 2; common #> SD sigma = 3. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96 (for two-sided alpha = #> 0.05), Z_beta = 0.8416 (for power = 0.80). #> • Step 4: Compute initial sample size via normal approximation: n0 = 2 * #> ((Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta) * sigma / delta)^2 = 2 * ((1.96 + 0.8416) * 3 / 2)^2 = #> 35.32. #> • Step 5: Refine via exact two-sample Student's t-test power iteration #> (accounting for degrees of freedom df = 2n - 2). #> • Step 6: Round up to integer: n = 37 per group, total sample size N = 74. #> Reference: #> Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). *Sample size calculations in clinical research* (3rd ed.). CRC Press. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> calculate("rct", "test", "proportion",   p1 = 0.85, p2 = 0.70 ) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Two independent proportions" #> • Sample size per group: 121 #> • Total sample size: 242 #> Formula (plain text): #> `n = (Z_a/2 * sqrt(2*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) + Z_b * sqrt(p1*(1-p1)+p2*(1-p2)))^2 / #> (p1-p2)^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n =  rac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{2 ar{p}(1- ar{p})} + Z_{ eta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1) + p_2(1-p_2)}ight]^2}{(p_1 - p_2)^2}$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State hypotheses: H0: p1 = p2 vs H1: p1 != p2 (two-sided alpha = #> 0.05, power = 0.80). #> • Step 2: Compute pooled proportion: p_bar = (p1 + p2) / 2 = (0.85 + 0.70) / 2 #> = 0.775. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416. #> • Step 4: Compute Fleiss formula numerator components: #> Z_(alpha/2)*sqrt(2*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) = 1.1575; Z_beta*sqrt(p1(1-p1)+p2(1-p2)) = #> 0.4889. #> • Step 5: Calculate unrounded sample size per group: n = (1.1575 + 0.4889)^2 / #> (0.85 - 0.70)^2 = 120.47. #> • Step 6: Round up to integer: n = 121 per group, total sample size N = 242. #> Reference: #> Primary (formula as implemented, without continuity correction): Fleiss, J. L., Tytun, A., & Ury, H. K. (1980). A simple approximation for calculating sample sizes for comparing independent proportions. Biometrics, 36(2), 343-346. #>  #> With continuity correction: Casagrande, J. T., Pike, M. C., & Smith, P. G. (1978). An improved approximate formula for calculating sample sizes for comparing two binomial distributions. Biometrics, 34(3), 483-494. #>  #> Book: Fleiss, J. L., Levin, B., & Paik, M. C. (2003). Statistical methods for rates and proportions (3rd ed.). Wiley. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> calculate("bioequivalence", "equivalence", "mean", cv = 0.25) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Bioequivalence (2x2 crossover, exact TOST noncentral t)" #> • Required sample size: 12 #> • Total sample size: 24 #> • Power achieved: 0.8372 #> Parameter roles #>  #> • cv = intra-subject coefficient of variation (log scale implied) #> • theta0 = anticipated geometric mean ratio (true ratio, default 1.0) #> • margin = [0.80, 1.25] average BE criteria #> • n is per sequence; total subjects = 2n #> Formula (plain text): #> `exact TOST (Phillips 1990): power = pt(-t, df, ncp=d2) - pt(t, df, ncp=d1)` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$	ext{Power} = F_t(-t_{1-\alpha,\, 
u};\, 
u,\, \delta_2) - F_t(t_{1-\alpha,\, 
u};\, 
u,\, \delta_1), \quad 
u = N-2$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: Intra-subject variance on log scale: sigma_w = sqrt(ln(1 + CV^2)) = #> sqrt(ln(1 + 0.25^2)) = 0.2462. #> • Step 2: Standard BE log-scale boundaries: [ln(0.80), ln(1.25)] = [-0.2231, #> 0.2231]. #> • Step 3: Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) under assumed geometric mean ratio theta0 #> = 1. #> • Step 4: Search sequence sample size n by evaluating the difference of #> noncentral t distribution probabilities (Phillips 1990; df = 2n - 2). #> • Step 5: Required sample size: n = 12 per sequence (achieved power = 0.8372, #> Total N = 24). #> Reference: #> Primary: Phillips, K. F. (1990). Power of the two one-sided tests procedure in bioequivalence. Journal of Pharmacokinetics and Biopharmaceutics, 18(2), 137-144. #>  #>  Also: Julious, S. A. (2004). Tutorial in biostatistics: sample sizes for clinical trials with normal data. Statistics in Medicine, 23, 1921-1986 (Eq 13, p. 1941); #>  Schuirmann, D. J. (1987). J Pharmacokinet Biopharm, 15(6), 657-680; #>  Chow & Liu (2009). Design and Analysis of Bioavailability and Bioequivalence Studies. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> calculate("diagAccuracy", "estimate", "proportion",   prob = 0.85, d = 0.05, prevalence = 0.2 ) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Diagnostic accuracy (single)" #> • Cases needed: 196 #> • Total subjects to screen: 980 #> • Total subjects: 980 #> Formula (plain text): #> `N_cases = (Z_1-a/2)^2 * P*(1-P)/d^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n_{{{cases}}} =  rac{Z_{1-\alpha/2}^2 \cdot p(1-p)}{d^2}$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: Specify diagnostic accuracy prob (Se or Sp) = 0.85, margin of error d #> = 0.05, prevalence = 0.20 (alpha = 0.05). #> • Step 2: Determine critical value: Z_(1-alpha/2) = 1.96 (confidence level = #> 95%). #> • Step 3: Calculate target cases required: n_cases = Z_sum^2 * prob * (1 - #> prob) / d^2 = (1.96)^2 * 0.85 * 0.15 / (0.05)^2 = 195.91. #> • Step 4: Adjust for disease prevalence: total subjects to screen = n_cases / #> prevalence = 195.91 / 0.20 = 979.57. #> • Step 5: Round up to integer: Target cases needed = 196, Total subjects to #> screen = 980. #> Reference: #> Primary: Hanley, J. A., & McNeil, B. J. (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143(1), 29-36. #>  #> Review: Hajian-Tilaki, K. (2014). Sample size estimation in diagnostic test studies of biomedical informatics. Journal of Biomedical Informatics, 48, 193-204. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> calculate("singleProportion", p = 0.30, precision = 0.05) # -> 323 #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Single proportion estimation (precision)" #> • Required sample size: 323 #> Parameter roles #>  #> • p = expected proportion (e.g. prevalence) #> • precision = margin of error d (half-width of the CI) #> • confidence level = 95% #> Formula (plain text): #> `n = Z^2 * p(1-p) / d^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n =  rac{Z_{1-\alpha/2}^2 \cdot p(1-p)}{d^2}$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: Specify anticipated proportion p = 0.30, margin of error d = 0.05 #> (absolute precision), alpha = 0.05. #> • Step 2: Determine critical value: Z_(1-alpha/2) = 1.96 (confidence level = #> 95%). #> • Step 3: Compute variance component: p * (1 - p) = 0.30 * 0.70 = 0.21. #> • Step 4: Calculate unrounded sample size: n = Z_(1-alpha/2)^2 * p * (1 - p) / #> d^2 = (1.96)^2 * 0.21 / (0.05)^2 = 322.68. #> • Step 5: Round up to integer: Required sample size n = 323. #> Reference: #> Bhardwaj et al. (2024). Determination of sample size for various study designs in medical research: A practical primer. Journal of Family Medicine and Primary Care, 13(7), 2555-2561 (p. 2558). #>  #> Also: Lwanga, S. K., & Lemeshow, S. (1991). Sample size determination in health studies: A practical manual. World Health Organization. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> calculate("diagAUC", auc = 0.80, d = 0.05) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Single-group AUC CI precision" #> Formula (plain text): #> `N_cases = (Z_1-a/2 / d)^2 * Var(AUC)` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n_{cases} = \left( rac{Z_{1-\alpha/2}}{d}ight)^2 \cdot Var(AUC)$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: Specify anticipated AUC = 0.80, desired precision d = 0.05, #> prevalence = 1 (alpha = 0.05). #> • Step 2: Hanley-McNeil variance components: Q1 = AUC/(2-AUC) = 0.6667, Q2 = #> 2*AUC^2/(1+AUC) = 0.7111. #> • Step 3: Compute variance factor: V(AUC) = Inf. #> • Step 4: Calculate cases needed: n_cases = (Z_(1-alpha/2) / d)^2 * V(AUC) = #> (1.96 / 0.05)^2 * Inf = Inf. #> • Step 5: Adjust for prevalence: screening total = n_cases / prevalence = Inf / #> 1 = Inf. #> • Step 6: Round up to integer: Target cases needed = Inf, Total subjects to #> screen = Inf. #> Reference: #> Primary: Hanley, J. A., & McNeil, B. J. (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143(1), 29-36. #>  #> Review: Hajian-Tilaki, K. (2014). Sample size estimation in diagnostic test studies of biomedical informatics. CRC Press. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>  sample_size_calculator("survival", hr = 0.7)                        # 247 events #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Survival (log-rank)" #> • Events needed: 247 #> Formula (plain text): #> `E = (Z_a/2 + Z_b)^2 / (pE*(1-pE)*log(HR)^2)` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$E = \frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta})^2}{p_E(1-p_E)[\ln(HR)]^2}$$ #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State survival parameters: Hazard Ratio HR = 0.70, experimental arm #> allocation pE = 0.50 (alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80). #> • Step 2: Compute log hazard ratio: ln(HR) = ln(0.70) = -0.3567. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416. #> • Step 4: Apply Schoenfeld formula: E = (Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta)^2 / [pE * (1 - #> pE) * (ln HR)^2] = (1.96 + 0.8416)^2 / [0.50 * 0.50 * (-0.3567)^2] = 246.79. #> • Step 5: Round up to integer: Target events needed E = 247. #> Reference: #> Primary: Schoenfeld, D. A. (1983). Sample-size formula for the proportional-hazards regression model. Biometrics, 39(2), 499-503. #>  #> Extensions: #> - Hsieh, F. Y., & Lavori, P. W. (2000). Sample-size calculations for the Cox proportional hazards regression model with nonbinary covariates. Controlled Clinical Trials, 21(6), 552-560. #> - Rubinstein, L. V., Gail, M. H., & Santner, T. J. (1981). Planning the duration of a comparative clinical trial with loss to follow-up and a period of continued observation. Journal of Chronic Diseases, 34(9-10), 469-479. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

title: Unified sample size calculator (three-axis API) — calculate
text: Object class sample_size_result print, summary, plot methods. Default printing shows sample sizes, plain-text formula (formula), LaTeX source (formula_latex), calculation process (calculation_steps, also available calculation), literature references (reference). New-style objects also carry axis metadata (task, outcome, design_canonical, results, roles, adjustments). summary.sample_size_result() additionally lists input parameters recorded adjustments.

text: n Cases per test; number >= 1. paired-patient design total number patients, imaged tests. J Number readers per test; integer >= 2 (F test needs J-1 df). delta Difference accuracy detect; number > 0 (AUC accuracy metric scale, e.g. 0.10). sigma_b2 -reader variance component; number >= 0. Planning heuristic: (accuracy range / 4)^2 (Zhou p. 223, Beam 1996). sigma_w2 Within-reader (occasion) variance component; number >= 0. sigma_c2 Patient-sampling (case) variance component; number >= 0 (e.g. 0.05 Zhou mammography example). rho1 Correlation, reader different tests; [0, 1). rho2 Correlation, different readers test; [0, 1). rho3 Correlation, different readers different tests; [0, 1). paired-patient, paired-reader parameterisation expects rho1 > rho2 > rho3 > 0 (Zhou Table 6.4); violated orderings warn. alpha Type error two-sided F test; (0, 1), default 0.05. n_repeats Reading occasions per reader-test (Q); integer >= 1, usually 1.

code: # Antihypertensive RCT: 37 patients per arm with these assumptions res <- calculate("rct", "test", "mean", mean1 = 10, mean2 = 12, sd = 3) print(res)   # sample sizes, both formulas, calculation process, references #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Two independent samples, mean comparison" #> • Sample size per group: 37 #> • Total sample size: 74 #> Formula (plain text): #> `n = 2 * ((Z_alpha/2 + Z_beta) * sd / (mean1 - mean2))^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n = 2\left(\frac{Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}}{\delta}\right)^2 = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}) \cdot \sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2}\right)^2$$  #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State hypotheses: H0: mu1 = mu2 vs H1: mu1 != mu2 (two-sided alpha = #> 0.05, power = 0.80). #> • Step 2: Calculate mean difference delta = |mu1 - mu2| = |10 - 12| = 2; common #> SD sigma = 3. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96 (for two-sided alpha = #> 0.05), Z_beta = 0.8416 (for power = 0.80). #> • Step 4: Compute initial sample size via normal approximation: n0 = 2 * #> ((Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta) * sigma / delta)^2 = 2 * ((1.96 + 0.8416) * 3 / 2)^2 = #> 35.32. #> • Step 5: Refine via exact two-sample Student's t-test power iteration #> (accounting for degrees of freedom df = 2n - 2). #> • Step 6: Round up to integer: n = 37 per group, total sample size N = 74. #> Reference: #> Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). *Sample size calculations in clinical research* (3rd ed.). CRC Press.  #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

code: # Antihypertensive RCT: 10 vs 12 mmHg SBP reduction, SD 3 -> 37 per arm sample_size_calculator("twoMeans", mean1 = 10, mean2 = 12, sd = 3) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Two independent samples, mean comparison" #> • Sample size per group: 37 #> • Total sample size: 74 #> Formula (plain text): #> `n = 2 * ((Z_alpha/2 + Z_beta) * sd / (mean1 - mean2))^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n = 2\left(\frac{Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}}{\delta}\right)^2 = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}) \cdot \sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2}\right)^2$$  #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State hypotheses: H0: mu1 = mu2 vs H1: mu1 != mu2 (two-sided alpha = #> 0.05, power = 0.80). #> • Step 2: Calculate mean difference delta = |mu1 - mu2| = |10 - 12| = 2; common #> SD sigma = 3. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96 (for two-sided alpha = #> 0.05), Z_beta = 0.8416 (for power = 0.80). #> • Step 4: Compute initial sample size via normal approximation: n0 = 2 * #> ((Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta) * sigma / delta)^2 = 2 * ((1.96 + 0.8416) * 3 / 2)^2 = #> 35.32. #> • Step 5: Refine via exact two-sample Student's t-test power iteration #> (accounting for degrees of freedom df = 2n - 2). #> • Step 6: Round up to integer: n = 37 per group, total sample size N = 74. #> Reference: #> Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). *Sample size calculations in clinical research* (3rd ed.). CRC Press.  #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>   # NSCLC immunotherapy trial: HR = 0.70, 1:1 allocation -> 247 events sample_size_calculator("survival", hr = 0.7, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Survival (log-rank)" #> • Events needed: 247 #> Formula (plain text): #> `E = (Z_a/2 + Z_b)^2 / (pE*(1-pE)*log(HR)^2)` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$E = \frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta})^2}{p_E(1-p_E)[\ln(HR)]^2}$$  #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State survival parameters: Hazard Ratio HR = 0.70, experimental arm #> allocation pE = 0.50 (alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80). #> • Step 2: Compute log hazard ratio: ln(HR) = ln(0.70) = -0.3567. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416. #> • Step 4: Apply Schoenfeld formula: E = (Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta)^2 / [pE * (1 - #> pE) * (ln HR)^2] = (1.96 + 0.8416)^2 / [0.50 * 0.50 * (-0.3567)^2] = 246.79. #> • Step 5: Round up to integer: Target events needed E = 247. #> Reference: #> Primary: Schoenfeld, D. A. (1983). Sample-size formula for the proportional-hazards regression model. Biometrics, 39(2), 499-503. #>  #> Extensions: #> - Hsieh, F. Y., & Lavori, P. W. (2000). Sample-size calculations for the Cox proportional hazards regression model with nonbinary covariates. Controlled Clinical Trials, 21(6), 552-560. #> - Rubinstein, L. V., Gail, M. H., & Santner, T. J. (1981). Planning the duration of a comparative clinical trial with loss to follow-up and a period of continued observation. Journal of Chronic Diseases, 34(9-10), 469-479.  #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>   # H. pylori eradication: quadruple 85% vs triple 70% -> 121 per arm sample_size_calculator("twoProportions", p1 = 0.85, p2 = 0.70) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results #> • Design type: "Two independent proportions" #> • Sample size per group: 121 #> • Total sample size: 242 #> Formula (plain text): #> `n = (Z_a/2 * sqrt(2*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) + Z_b * sqrt(p1*(1-p1)+p2*(1-p2)))^2 / #> (p1-p2)^2` #> Formula (LaTeX): #> $$n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{2\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1) + p_2(1-p_2)}\right]^2}{(p_1 - p_2)^2}$$  #> Calculation process: #>  #> • Step 1: State hypotheses: H0: p1 = p2 vs H1: p1 != p2 (two-sided alpha = #> 0.05, power = 0.80). #> • Step 2: Compute pooled proportion: p_bar = (p1 + p2) / 2 = (0.85 + 0.70) / 2 #> = 0.775. #> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416. #> • Step 4: Compute Fleiss formula numerator components: #> Z_(alpha/2)*sqrt(2*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) = 1.1575; Z_beta*sqrt(p1(1-p1)+p2(1-p2)) = #> 0.4889. #> • Step 5: Calculate unrounded sample size per group: n = (1.1575 + 0.4889)^2 / #> (0.85 - 0.70)^2 = 120.47. #> • Step 6: Round up to integer: n = 121 per group, total sample size N = 242. #> Reference: #> Primary (formula as implemented, without continuity correction): Fleiss, J. L., Tytun, A., & Ury, H. K. (1980). A simple approximation for calculating sample sizes for comparing independent proportions. Biometrics, 36(2), 343-346. #>  #> With continuity correction: Casagrande, J. T., Pike, M. C., & Smith, P. G. (1978). An improved approximate formula for calculating sample sizes for comparing two binomial distributions. Biometrics, 34(3), 483-494. #>  #> Book: Fleiss, J. L., Levin, B., & Paik, M. C. (2003). Statistical methods for rates and proportions (3rd ed.). Wiley.  #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>

title: sampleSizeCalc 3.1.1 (Development)
text: singleCorrelation: Fixed implementation strictly match Machin et al. (2018, Chapter 19, Equations 19.5-19.8). Now supports precision (absolute CI half-width) epsilon (relative precision). Produces exact agreement presize::prec_cor (e.g., r=0.5, conf.width=0.10 -> 867; r=0.5, conf.width=0.20 -> 219). bioequivalence: Upgraded 2x2 crossover TOST crude normal approximation exact noncentral t distribution (Phillips 1990; Julious 2004 Equation 13). Added support theta0 (expected geometric mean ratio, default 1.0) custom equivalence bounds (margin_low, margin_high). Results match PowerTOST::sampleN.TOST bit--bit (e.g., CV=0.25, theta0=1.0 -> N=24, 12/sequence; theta0=0.95 -> N=28, 14/sequence). diagAccuracy (test): Added method = c("asymptotic", "exact"). Setting method = "exact" executes exact binomial search per ’Hern (2001), returning critical successes critical_successes alongside sample size (e.g., prob=0.85, p0=0.70 gives n=49, critical cutoff r=40). steppedWedge: Explicit warning regarding absence calendar-time fixed effects Hussey & Hughes (2007) Equation 8 potential power loss. singleArmPhaseII: Documented ties minimax total N broken minimizing Type error alpha. caseControlMatched: Clarified psi discordant pair proportion (pi10 + pi01), discordant odds ratio. cohortRate: Clarified required subjects = person-time / follow-duration. diagLR: Clarified sample size ensures CI cross target_lr, distinct fixed-width CI estimation.

title: sampleSizeCalc 3.1.0
text: predictiveModel + task=“plan” + outcome=“binary”: Riley 2020 BMJ method prediction model development sample size (original paper obtained implemented). Criteria B1 (outcome proportion precision), B3 (shrinkage target via Cox-Snell R2), B2 (van Smeden MAPE, P <= 30) entropy-based max R2cs helper. Anchors exact: B3 P=30/R2cs=0.05/S=0.9 -> 5249 (matches pmsampsize), B1 phi=0.5/delta=0.05 -> 385, B2 MAPE=0.05/ phi=0.3/P=10 -> 461 (Fig 2 worked example). predictiveModel + task=“plan” + outcome=“rate”: Riley 2020 criterion T1 time--event outcomes — person-years follow-needed precise cumulative incidence exponential model (exact binomial-CI search; anchor: rate=0.10/yr, t=10y, delta=0.05 -> 2366 person-years, exactly paper’s Figure 1 worked example). mrmc_power(): power calculation MRMC studies (paired-patient, paired-reader) using Obuchowski-Rockette mixed model / non-central F framework (Zhou et al. 2011 Eq 6.32, Tables 6.3-6.4). Verified book’s mammography worked example (power ~= 0.89 n=50, J=8, delta=0.10). steppedWedge + task=“test”: Hussey-Hughes Eq 8 WLS Wald power full stepped wedge designs (original paper obtained Eq 8 implemented directly; EPT figure-read anchor discrepancy documented — Eq 8 gives power 0.959 RR=0.64 80% crossing RR=0.73). kappa + task=“estimate”/“test”: Cohen’s kappa sample size per Cantor (1996), using Fleiss-Cohen-Everitt variance factor Q = po(1-po)/(1-pe)^2. Anchors exact: Q(0.5,0.5,0.7) = 0.510 two-questionnaire test N = 214. (Table 1/2 QMAX values require full FCE lambda1 term; estimate mode conditional planning kappa.)

title: sampleSizeCalc 3.1.0
text: clusterRCT + task=“test” + outcome=“mean”/“proportion”: design-effect wrapper (DE = 1+(m-1)ICC) around individually-randomised kernels, cluster-level rounding (n_clusters per arm = ceil(nDE/m)) (Machin 2018 Ch.12; Donner & Klar 2000). singleArmPhaseII: exact Simon two-stage designs (optimal = min E[N|p0], minimax = min N) via vectorised exact binomial search (Simon 1989), plus ’Hern single-stage (’Hern 2001). Anchors verified Machin 2018 Chapter 17: optimal (1/10, 5/29) ’Hern 6/25, 12/35 reproduced exactly; book’s minimax (2/15, 5/25) exact power 0.7696 < 0.80 strict definition excluded (documented discrepancy). rct + task=“noninferiority” + outcome=“proportion”: fills legacy margin gap (nonInferiorityProportions). twoOrdinal: ordered categorical two-group comparison via Whitehead’s formula N = 3(Za/2+Zb)2/((logOR)2(1-sum(p^3))) (Whitehead 1993; Machin 2018 Ch.4). predictiveModel + task=“plan”: events-per-variable rule (EPV >= 10, Peduzzi 1996) pointer Riley et al. (2019). + task=“test”: interrupted time series level-change power AR(1) effective-sample-size correction - marked EXPERIMENTAL output hints (framework: Bernal et al. 2017; transparent approximation, validated source formula). Deferred documented reasons: kappa steppedWedge (Machin Ch.20/Ch.13 formulas OCR-garbled available PDF; require paper derivation implementation).

title: sampleSizeCalc 3.1.0
text: diagAccuracyCompare + task=“noninferiority”/“equivalence”: two- proportion margin framework one-sided alpha NI Z_{beta/2} equivalence, plus prevalence screening conversion. diagAUCCompare + task=“noninferiority”/“equivalence”: margin framework AUC difference correlation r three variance functions (framework per Chow et al. 2017; application per Zhou 2011 Section 6.3). diagAccuracyCompare + paired=TRUE via three-axis API now uses Connor kernel psi = discordant-pair PROPORTION (legacy keyword keeps old sqrt-scale parameterization, locked test). crossover: 2x2 crossover within-subject SD parameterization (n = 2(Za/2+Zb)^2 sigma_w^2 / delta^2; Senn 2002). bioequivalence: 2x2 TOST log scale, 80-125% criterion (n = 2(Z_{1-}+Z_{1-b})^2 log(1+CV2)/log(1.25)2; Schuirmann 1987; Julious 2004), replicate-design hint CV > 30%. diagAccuracy + dual=TRUE: dual-endpoint strategy computing sensitivity specificity requirements dual_power (default 0.90 -> ~80% joint) taking max (Akoglu 2022 p.184). Dispatcher gains path flag (“legacy” vs “three-axis”) upgrades can diverge cleanly locked legacy behavior.

title: sampleSizeCalc 3.1.0
text: cohort + task=“test” + outcome=“proportion”: exposed vs unexposed cumulative incidence 1:m allocation (ratio), optional dropout inflation, RR parameter roles (Bhardwaj 2024 p.2559 anchor; exact-z value 294, paper’s rounded-z 293, ±1 documented). cohort + outcome=“rate”: person-time incidence-rate comparison unequal allocation (Machin 2018 Ch.6; IRR roles). caseControlMatched: individually matched 1:1 case-control via discordant-pairs formulation independence-within-pair approximation (Dupont 1988; Schlesselman 1982 p.174). crosstab: cross-sectional prevalence comparison (PR/roles), sharing two-proportion kernel. paired + outcome=“proportion”: McNemar/Connor paired binary kernel explicit discordant-pair proportion psi (Connor 1987; Akoglu 2022 Table 6A uncorrected anchor 155 psi = delta = 0.05, 80% power). rctSingleArm + task=“test”: single-arm vs fixed value mean (Machin Ch.5) proportion outcomes (Hajian-Tilaki Eq 6.8 anchor 153). inflate_n() gains method = "additive" (n*(1+d), matching arithmetic Bhardwaj worked examples) alongside canonical “inflate” (n/(1-d)). Result objects promote new metric fields: n_exposed, n_unexposed, person_time_exposed, person_time_unexposed, expected_events, n_pairs.

title: sampleSizeCalc 3.1.0
text: singleProportion: precision-based n = Z2*p(1-p)/d2 absolute relative precision extreme-prevalence convention hints (Bhardwaj 2024 p.2558; anchor 323). singleMean: n = (Z*sigma/d)^2 (Machin 2018 Ch.9). singleCorrelation: Fisher-z precision n = ((1+r2)/(r*eps))2 + 3 (Machin 2018 Ch.19). diagAccuracy + ci_method: “precision” (Zhou Eq 6.2) “ci_width_power” (Zhou Eq 6.1, Flahault 2005; anchors 246/503). diagAUC + var_method: “exponential” (Zhou Eq 6.4), “binormal” (Obuchowski 1994, Zhou Eq 6.5; CTC anchor 46/92), “conservative” (distribution-free, Zhou Eq 6.6; anchor 62/123); plus explicit case: control ratio parameter. diagLR + lr_type/target_lr: log-LR CI method (Hajian-Tilaki 2014 Sections 6.4, Eqs 6.13/6.14) replacing simplified Se/Sp-max formula new-style calls. New exported utility screen_required(n, prevalence, beta): total screening enrollment exact binomial probability guarantee capturing n cases (Zhou 2011 Eq 6.3; anchor 451 350 cases, 80% prevalence, 90% guarantee). Result objects gain hints (methodological warnings surfaced user) n_required (single-sample estimation results).
